deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text by Grothendieck. It is a sheet of recycled IBM line-printer paper carrying CEA Cadarache JESNEWS bulletins dated 09/08/1982 and 18/08/1982. Over this printout Grothendieck drew a series of discs, each standing for the projective plane modelled as a disc with antipodal boundary identification, or for a disc chart of it. The discs contain arrangements of pseudolines drawn in orange felt pen.

The small discs show elementary configurations:
- Two curves crossing once, with a third pencil arc (black) closing a triangle-like cell; a dot marks a cell.
- Two or three pseudolines crossing in a larger pencil-drawn disc.
- Half-discs or lunes cut by a few arcs.
- A disc with two shaded orange triangles meeting at a crossing (an 'hourglass'). This is evidently a picture of a triangular cell before and after a local move, or of the two triangles adjacent to a vertex.

The upper-right disc shows a 'generic' arrangement of about ten orange pseudolines. Some boundary cells are hatched in pencil, presumably marking cells of a given type, such as triangles or cells touching the line at infinity.

The large lower-right disc shows about eight orange pseudolines with all their crossing points marked by dots. Endpoints on the boundary circle carry numerical labels (roughly 8, 12, 2, 1(?), 15, 14/16, 9, 5, 6, 18, 2, 1). Superimposed on the orange lines is a dense family of green curves running roughly 'vertically'. They are mutually nested and appear to cross each orange line once. Pencil hatching marks some cells, and small 'm'-shaped scribbles appear where the green curves pass near crossings.

In context, the next page discusses 'balayage', 'antibalayage', transition arcs, specialization/generalization arcs and an operation of rotation ρ(D,ω,a). The green family is therefore most plausibly a sweep of the arrangement by a moving pseudoline (a 'pencil' of sweep curves). Each green curve is a position of a sweeping pseudoline, and successive positions differ by passing over one vertex. This is the combinatorial device behind wiring diagrams and topological sweeps, and behind Grothendieck's study of 'positions relatives' D and the moves between them (triangle flips = Ringel moves, or passing a sweep line across a vertex). The numerical labels likely index the lines or their points at infinity, so the order of crossings along each sweep position can be read off.

The page thus serves as experimental drawing for the theory of relative positions of pseudoline systems and their elementary transitions, developed in words on the following page.
errors: No mathematical statements to check; the drawings are exploratory. It cannot be verified from the image that every green curve meets every orange curve exactly once. Some green curves appear to bend sharply near crossings, so a few may not be genuine pseudolines of the extended arrangement.

ideas.what: Arrangements of pseudolines in the projective plane drawn in a disc model, with crossing points marked and lines labelled at infinity
A family of nested curves sweeping across an arrangement, each crossing every pseudoline once (sweeping/balayage), linked to transitions between relative positions
ideas.modern_name: topological sweep of pseudoline arrangements; wiring diagrams; extension by a pencil
ideas.usually_credited_to: Goodman (1980, wiring diagrams), Edelsbrunner–Guibas (1986, topological sweep), Snoeyink–Hershberger (1989, sweeping arrangements of curves)

ideas.what: Shaded triangular cells / hourglass configuration at a crossing, i.e. local triangle moves between arrangements

deep.surprise_reason: Purely illustrative drawings of pseudoline arrangements and an apparent sweep, matching standard notions (wiring diagrams, topological sweep, Ringel flips). The only curiosity is that Grothendieck independently used sweeping ideas in 1983–84, around the same time as the computational-geometry literature. Nothing on the page goes beyond known results.
transcription_corrections: The endpoint labels on the large disc are hard to read. The right-side label rendered as '16' looks more like '14' (written '1b'), and the label rendered 't' at the upper left is probably '1' or '7'. Lower-left 'b' is likely '6', and right-side ',5' may be '15'.
The small left label near the half-disc reads '5' (also mirrored); the faint pencil label at the bottom centre near the edge looks like '1' and '4'.
The printout header reads 'C68 CADARACHE' (i.e. 168, the IBM 370/168), and the 'p. 102' numbering is pencilled at the bottom left.
